title: "Decision History"

# Decision History

Every feature this project has shipped through its specification process, condensed into
one story: what each set out to achieve, why it mattered, where later decisions undid or
refined an earlier one, and what we learned along the way. It favors judgment over
procedure — for step-by-step acceptance gates from before this process existed, read the
[development notes](developer_notes/index.qmd); for the design of the system *as it stands
today*, read [architecture](dev/architecture.qmd) and [seams](dev/seams.qmd).

The twelve features fall into three arcs: the agent surface taking shape, the AI plumbing
industrializing, and platform polish. Within each arc the entries flow chronologically;
reversals are stated openly wherever they happened — including two decisions that were
built and then replaced inside their own feature before landing.

## Arc A — The agent surface takes shape

Mayon gained its first external tool, then rebuilt the surface where tool activity
appears. A web-search integration produced a flood of raw tool rows; typed timeline
entries made that flood legible; live use exposed what fixtures could not catch; and a
contract pass converged every assistant-initiated interaction into one governed place.

## 001 — Brave Search MCP service

> **Status:** standing (its credential/topology design was revised twice within the
> feature itself, before release)

**Goal.** Give the assistant web search through the official Brave Search MCP server as
Mayon's first external tool integration. A self-hoster adds a "Brave Search" connection
like any other MCP server, and during conversation the model consults search whenever a
question touches something recent or fast-moving that its training data cannot answer
reliably. Every reply that drew on results displays its consulted sources as links, so
answers become checkable rather than stale guesses. Success criteria set the bar: a
healthy connection within two minutes of opening settings, at least 90% correct answers
on twenty post-training-cutoff questions, sources visible on 100% of search-backed
replies, and graceful degradation — normal chat completes with an unobtrusive notice
whenever search is down, disabled, or out of quota.

**Why.** The requester's recorded rationale is explicit: model knowledge goes stale and
external validation is the only cure, and the compose-based deployment made adding a
component cheap. Without it, any question about events after the model's cutoff got an
unverifiable answer. Privacy shaped the design too: third-party-hosted Brave endpoints
put the API key into URL query parameters and interpose an intermediary, so the spec
demanded a private path where the key never appears in a URL, settings, or logs.

**Outcome & reversals.** The feature shipped twice in one day. Research established that
the official package accepts its API key only at process startup, so the first shipped
design was a dedicated companion container holding the key as deployment configuration,
reached browser-to-container through a same-origin streaming proxy route on the Mayon
server and gated by a new capability flag. The same day, the owner revised the
requirement: all credentials must live in one place, the app's existing keystore.
Everything container-specific — compose service, proxy route, capability, HTTP template —
was removed, and Brave became a plain stdio template: the Mayon server spawns the pinned
package per session, injecting the key from the browser keystore at spawn time. Key
rotation applies next turn with no restarts; an invalid key surfaces only when a search
runs, since the handshake succeeds regardless. Retained from the container iteration were
the transport-agnostic pieces: the citations extractor rendering source links from
already-persisted tool-result metadata (zero migrations, retroactive for old chats),
degradation/recovery tests, and root-relative URL support. Accepted cost: a one-to-three-
second per-session spawn while enabled.

**Learnings.**

- An upstream constraint does not dictate topology: for a spawned child, spawn time *is*
  startup, so keystore-to-env injection reconciles unified secret custody with the key's
  startup-only injection.
- Derive view-only data from already-persisted metadata when a single consumer exists —
  no migrations, and history upgrades retroactively.
- Work built for a reverted design is not waste if kept general; URL support and
  degradation tests outlived the proxy, capability, and container.
- One consistent secret home for all MCP servers beat a leaner deployment with split
  custody.

## 002 — Chat timeline kind model

> **Status:** core standing; presentation rules partly superseded by
> [#004](#sec-004) (live-item placement and stream-buffer retirement only)

**Goal.** Replace the timeline's implied content model — provider intent and UI
presentation both guessed from nullable column combinations — with one explicit durable
`kind` per timeline event from a closed ten-value enum. Lane (user/internal/external)
becomes a pure derivation from kind, never stored; a single kind→presentation registry
drives every renderer for persisted rows and live streaming alike; permission, sampling,
and elicitation asks persist with resolved outcomes surviving reload; choice offers
persist with the tapped chip linked back; reasoning persists per agent-loop iteration;
critic corrections record a self-corrected note. Context assembly becomes a pure
entries→provider-messages projection locked to prior behavior by golden tests. Storage
evolves in place: an additive column plus a stamped migration backfilling every legacy
row.

**Why.** The verified pre-existing facts were damning: approval asks lived in ephemeral
in-memory arrays and vanished on reload; reasoning from all iterations accumulated into
one buffer glued onto the final assistant row, misattributing thinking; the render ladder
hid blank bookkeeping rows through scattered special cases; tool-heavy turns produced a
wall of muted text; and context assembly re-guessed provider intent from the same
ambiguous columns the UI guessed from — a standing invitation to divergence between what
the user sees and what the model receives.

**Outcome & reversals.** Delivered in full across five stories. The legacy render ladder
was deleted in favor of per-kind renderers dispatched through the registry; a boot-time
migration runner was added (research found version-stamped upgrades previously had no
consumer that ran data migrations); the backfill classifies 100% of legacy rows and fails
loudly on unmatched shapes, preserving row IDs so branch points and expound offsets stay
valid; full-text search was deliberately tightened to user/assistant kinds — tool
summaries were searchable noise before; new-turn choices collapse from a hidden tool-call
pair into one offer entry linked to the tapped chip. One quirk was deliberately preserved:
replayed tool calls project with empty input because the old gather step never populated
args — "flag, don't fix" to keep golden equivalence. Later refinement: feature
[#004](#sec-004) replaced the rule that live items always append after durable ones,
moving stream-buffer retirement into the store at tool-call boundaries and merging pending
asks to their durable row's chronological position.

**Learnings.**

- Intent inferred from nullable column combinations rots independently in every consumer;
  one explicit kind fixed UI, migration, and projection at once.
- Snapshot golden fixtures from current code *before* rewriting the seam they protect —
  equivalence claims need a prior baseline to compare against.
- Earn constraints: backfill everything first, then enforce non-null — silent defaults
  mask exactly the rot the migration exists to classify.
- Phase risk down: ship new semantics as runtime derivation first, land storage second.

One day of live use against the new registry surfaced four defects no fixture caught —
the agenda for the next feature.

## 003 — Timeline UX fixes

> **Status:** standing

**Goal.** Fix four defects reported against the freshly shipped timeline: (1) the orbit
spinner spun forever on finished replies, persisting after reload; (2) turn order rendered
the reply before its thought process, violating canonical chronological order — reasoning,
then assistant text, then tool activity; (3) terminal tools such as the choices presenter
ended the turn by design yet displayed a failure icon and "No Result Recorded"; (4) the
diagnostics panel crashed whenever an MCP server connected and disconnected in one
session, blocking users from opening chats at all. Each fix ships with a regression test
that fails without it.

**Why.** These were the first real-world verdicts on the kind registry. The permanent
spinner trained users to ignore genuine progress signals. Misordered renders read as
dishonest history — the exact failure mode the kind model was built to eliminate. And the
diagnostics crash took priority purely operationally: it destroyed the reporting channel
the other three bugs depended on.

**Outcome & reversals.** All four landed as presentation-layer surgery plus one
persist-order correction, with no schema change and golden provider-context tests passing
unmodified. Root-causing the third defect revealed deeper rot: the agent loop persisted
tool iterations out of order, and worse, the tool-pairing map was keyed by row id instead
of tool-call id — meaning **no production tool pair had ever grouped**, invisible because
test fixtures set both fields to identical strings. The fixes: persist reasoning first per
iteration; key pairing correctly; drop the end-of-timeline flush that fabricated false
chronology; add a stable within-turn reorder pass that repairs wrongly-stored history
without touching stored data. Later features extended this work:
[#004](#sec-004) taught awaiting-approval calls to read as pending rather than failed, and
[#005](#sec-005) rebuilt the expanded result body.

**Learnings.**

- Never let fixture identifiers equal their join keys — synthetic equality masked a
  production-wide pairing failure.
- Pair a presentation-time repair pass (fixes historical display without data writes) with
  persist-order fixes (stop manufacturing bad history going forward).
- Classification belongs to one registry; a UI-maintained tool-name list drifts the moment
  the backend changes.
- Availability of the bug-reporting path ranks above UX polish in triage.

With kinds, ordering, and pairing sound, the first real MCP server — whose risky calls
need human approval — exposed honesty gaps that only a contract-level pass could close.

## 004 — Internal area unification

> **Status:** contracts standing; result-body presentation section superseded by
> [#005](#sec-005)

**Goal.** The third iteration on the chat surface closed five verified defect classes
exposed by one live MCP tool-call turn, and converged all assistant-initiated interaction
into the timeline's internal lane: an assistant text segment renders exactly once across
the streaming→persisted boundary; a tool call awaiting approval reads as waiting, not
failed; results render collapsed with a one-line summary; approvals, sampling asks, and
elicitation offers live at their chronological position while the composer stays strictly
user-input-only; and the captured request trace mirrors what was actually sent to the
provider. Four written contracts came out of it — timeline assembly, tool activity status,
interactive surfaces, request trace — with zero schema change.

**Why.** Live use proved the timeline could lie. Persisted text kept rendering again from
a stale stream buffer until turn end — a duplicate that fixed itself only after approval.
A pending approval showed two ask surfaces at once while its tool row wore a failure icon,
actively convincing the reporter something had errored. Multi-part MCP search results
dumped as a wall of raw JSON. Pacing chips sat in the composer, asks at the tail, choices
in the lane — three places answering one need. Worst, the diagnostics trace duplicated the
system prompt and stripped tool identity, making users suspect double-sent context. At
stake was trust in every approval wait.

**Outcome & reversals.** All shipped presentation-layer: no migrations, one additive field
on new tool-result metadata, golden provider-context tests unmodified. Three contracts
stand today: no assistant-initiated interaction may ever be added to the composer — pacing
offers are tappable on the timeline's choices offer, overriding the earlier rule
([#002](#sec-002)) that live items simply append after durable rows; tool activity
statuses derive at render time from stored rows, live state, and the registry — never
stored; and the request trace mirrors only the projected wire payload. Within days, the
collapsed-result body section (truncated summary plus floating expander) was replaced by
[#005](#sec-005)'s shape-driven renderer, which explicitly supersedes that contract section
while keeping collapse-by-default intact.

**Learnings.**

- Retire live state at the persist choke point; content-matching dedupe at assembly hides
  staleness instead of fixing it.
- Derive display states, never store them — a pure function of stored rows, live state,
  and registry is testable and migration-free.
- Diagnostics that log transformed data lie; log the wire payload itself.
- Interaction placement is a contract, not styling: writing down "composer = user input
  only" is what prevents slow regression.

That collapse fix also exposed the next gap: hiding the payload was easy, but whatever
appeared on expand still read like a wall.

*Arc A in retrospect:* the surface learned to tell the truth in layers — first structural
truth (typed entries), then behavioral truth (ordering, pairing), then contractual truth
(where interaction may live and what diagnostics may say). Every later arc inherited those
contracts instead of rediscovering them.

## Arc B — The AI plumbing industrializes

Results learned to render by shape rather than server identity, bespoke UI gave way to
adopted community patterns, provider onboarding turned into catalog data, request
behavior centralized into one resolution seam, and study controls opened up without
touching fragile geometry.

## 005 — Shape-driven tool result rendering

> **Status:** standing

**Goal.** Make expanded tool-result bodies readable by classifying each result through
one pure classifier returning exactly one shape — records, JSON, markdown, text, or short
prose — and rendering accordingly: URL-bearing records become a capped list of link cards
with the separate sources list folded in; markdown renders as markdown; other JSON
pretty-prints; anything unrecognized degrades to today's bounded raw view. Classification
precedence is fixed, tolerant of multi-part payloads joined without separators. Strictly
presentation-only: stored payloads are read-only inputs, so legacy chats render nicely
with zero data change.

**Why.** MCP mount code joins content parts with no separator, so concatenated JSON is
the normal case, and nothing between storage and screen parsed it. The same payload was
parsed again for the sources link list — links shown twice, once as a wall. Meanwhile the
constitution forbids UI-side per-tool special cases, ruling out hand-maintained branches
by tool name or server. Identity-blind shape detection was the only road that scales.

**Outcome & reversals.** Standing today: the classifier is named the single shape
authority in the current architecture docs — never tool identity, never a UI-side tool
list — with degradation structural: the raw view is the ladder's bottom rung, not an error
boundary around rendering. It replaced feature [#004](#sec-004)'s result-body expander
section and swapped the floating toggle for the header row itself; for record shapes the
sources row is suppressed so exactly one list renders — partially retiring the separate
Sources list that [#001](#sec-001) had introduced (it survives for other shapes). Feature
[#006](#sec-006) retained the body renderer untouched inside its new collapsible shell and
deliberately skipped a donor code-highlighting block to avoid a second path — a direct
endorsement. Nothing later overturns it.

**Learnings.**

- Classify payload shape, never tool identity: shape-based rendering survives every new
  tool without registry coupling.
- Build graceful degradation structurally — make the old-correct view the ladder's bottom
  rung instead of wrapping rendering in error handling.
- Share parsers between consumers so two views can never disagree about the payload.
- Read actual storage shape before designing APIs: a spec'd nested-field read would have
  silently seen nothing for every real row.

## 006 — AI elements adoption

> **Status:** standing

**Goal.** Converge three leaf UI surfaces onto community consensus patterns by copying
donor blocks from the Svelte AI Elements registry into the repo as first-party code —
trimmed, locally owned, no runtime dependency: a searchable command-palette model picker
replacing the hand-rolled dropdown; one shared confirmation pattern unifying elicitation
and sampling approval; and a collapsible tool-call shell for transcript rows. Constraint
terms: zero new packages — donors depend only on libraries already present — plus four
dependency-free vocabulary primitives added. The message render path, expound highlighting,
and branching stayed deliberately hand-maintained.

**Why.** Maintenance cost concentrated in hand-built interaction logic nobody wanted to
own. The picker was the largest hand-maintained component with real accessibility gaps:
no arrow-key navigation, no escape handling, no focus management. Elicitation dialog and
sampling card were two bespoke surfaces answering one safety-critical UX. Aligning on
widely-used patterns buys familiarity and community-hardened keyboard behavior while
deleting bespoke code.

**Outcome & reversals.** All three surfaces shipped; the dependency-manifest diff stayed
empty end-to-end. An honest miss recorded rather than hidden: the success criterion
required net custom UI code to shrink against its baseline, but the ledger shows growth —
justified line-by-line as capabilities the old code lacked (keyboard nav, focus trap,
failure badges, a failed terminal state, genuine deduplication). The ledger's argument:
the risk actually being targeted — hand-rolled outside-click handlers, ad-hoc state spans
— measurably retired. Adoption trade-offs held: donor auto-open behavior dropped, logos
trimmed, domain-specific schema forms kept where generic blocks don't fit. Later features
extended the picker's list rather than replacing it.

**Learnings.**

- Copy-in adoption harvests consensus behavior without registry dependency risk — but
  "net less code" is the wrong success metric; count retired interaction logic instead.
- Adapt donors aggressively: replace helpers, delete unwanted behaviors, keep domain forms.
- Vocabulary primitives amortize beyond the triggering feature; ledger them separately or
  bundle-size rules punish doing the right thing.

With the interaction surface settled, the same industrializing instinct turned to the
provider side of the wire — where manual endpoint entry had become the bottleneck.

## 007 — First-class inference provider templates

> **Status:** standing

**Goal.** Promote six high-demand inference providers — DeepSeek, xAI Grok, Moonshot
Kimi, Qwen/DashScope, Groq, Mistral — from manual custom-endpoint setup to first-class
one-click entries: paste an API key, pick a model, chat with tool calling on by default,
in under two minutes without typing an endpoint address or reading provider docs.

**Why.** All six were reachable only through the generic OpenAI-compatible escape hatch,
which demanded knowing each endpoint address and tool-calling implications. Usage evidence
showed DeepSeek alone carrying more weekly routed usage than Google and OpenAI combined.
Following the project's Pareto rule for provider support, six promotions were selected and
ordered by measured demand. Everything outside stayed deliberately template-free.

**Outcome & reversals.** Shipped as pure catalog data: six template constants, gateway
URLs added to the exact-string tool-defaulting set — including regional variants and alias
spellings — curated fallback model lists snapshotted at implementation time. No new
dependency, transport, auth flow, or UI component (a success criterion made that
verifiable). One designed non-outcome: whether DashScope exposes a model listing was
probed live during implementation and answered no, so Qwen ships a curated list instead of
live discovery — the spec had pre-approved both outcomes. Automated order tests passed;
per-provider end-to-end chats needing real keys were logged as requiring user validation.
Standing: feature [#008](#sec-008) appends downstream in the same array and
[#009](#sec-009) left templates untouched.

**Learnings.**

- When candidates share one wire format, provider onboarding industrializes into data
  entry on existing machinery.
- Exact-string URL matching forces enumeration of every valid spelling — undocumented
  variants would silently lose tools-on-by-default.
- Curated fallback model lists go stale by design: snapshot at implementation, let live
  discovery supersede them.
- Frame verification questions so either answer ships: the DashScope probe had both
  outcomes pre-specified, requiring no re-planning.

## 008 — First-class inference router templates

> **Status:** standing

**Goal.** Extend the one-click treatment from direct providers to inference routers —
services fronting many upstream models behind one endpoint: a curated coding-agent
gateway with a free tier, self-hosted LiteLLM, a zero-markup hosted gateway, and an
EU-endpoint router — alongside the existing OpenRouter and Kilo Gateway entries.

**Why.** Companion research identified four high-audience routers users could only reach
via manual custom endpoints. LiteLLM mattered doubly: it is the de-facto self-hosted
gateway of Mayon's audience, and the sanctioned path to enterprise-cloud models — cloud
credentials stay server-side inside the user's own gateway, so Mayon ever sees only
standard wire format. Direct enterprise integrations remained explicit non-goals.

**Outcome & reversals.** Shipped in roughly half a day: four templates appended after the
direct-provider block (order tests extended, catalog grew to seventeen), more gateway URLs
added, and — the single runtime change — discovery now skips entries typed as embedding:
a conservative one-value denylist protecting discoverable providers from mixed catalogs,
provably leaving untyped catalogs unchanged. LiteLLM became the first hosted template with
no required key, reusing Ollama's keyless flow: setup completes without a key prompt,
anonymous discovery works, and a key saved later upgrades the connection. Its fallback
list ships intentionally wrong placeholders: for a private gateway, the user's own
configured aliases are the only real catalog. Documented rough edge rather than solved:
inside Mayon's containerized server, localhost resolves within the container, so docs
point self-hosted-gateway users at the docker host address — an address edit, not
auto-detection. No reversals; feature [#009](#sec-009) routes router-prefixed model ids
through last-segment matching instead of adding router dialect rows.

**Learnings.**

- Delegation beats accumulation: one self-hosted-gateway template covers arbitrarily many
  upstreams, including clouds whose auth flows Mayon will never implement.
- Append template cohorts as contiguous demand-ordered blocks; order stays meaningful and
  tests extend instead of rewriting.
- Discovery filters should be denylists grown only on observed evidence; an allowlist
  would have emptied the many untyped catalogs.
- Keyless support is positive capability design — skip the prompt, discover anonymously,
  upgrade later.

Direct providers and routers could now be added without code — but the parameters each
request carried were still hard-coded and, for newer models, broken.

## 009 — Provider request settings

> **Status:** standing (today's single request-settings seam, confirmed by current
> architecture docs)

**Goal.** Decide every outgoing model request's parameters through one shared, testable
mechanism: a static dialect catalog plus a pure resolver producing top-level call
settings, provider-namespaced body options, and a dropped-keys list; two new optional user
fields on provider config — sampling defaults and a validated raw extra-body passthrough —
applied identically across all four call paths (chat, critic correction pass, lab/quiz
generation, title generation) and rendered in traces plus a settings preview.

**Why.** Users controlled exactly one knob — the reasoning toggle — and it worked only
for unprefixed GLM ids: prefixed ids via routers silently lost their mapping. Sampling
control did not exist, and mapping data was stale: Anthropic rejected the emitted
deprecated form outright, Gemini switched parameter names, Groq leaked raw think tags, and
three providers needed entirely new forms.

**Outcome & reversals.** Shipped with replacement at its core: the previous reasoning-map
functions were deleted outright (zero references remained). Resolution layers, each
overriding the last: kind baseline → endpoint dialect matched on base URL → model overlay
matched on the model id's last segment → user sampling defaults → validated extra body,
where the user wins. It builds on features [#007](#sec-007)/[#008](#sec-008) — registry
pinned unchanged, dialect rows attach to the same catalog, routers need none. Research
surfaced two silent-defect fixes folded in: the options namespace key must mirror how the
SDK itself derives it (case-preserved, dot-truncating); the old lowercasing meant the SDK
consumed nothing, silently dropping all reasoning parameters for template-named providers,
and because of that the old baseline had been junk-emitting empty thinking objects to
every compatible endpoint undetected — so the baseline now invents nothing, with previously
served endpoints re-served by dialect tables; separately, Gemini's thinking configuration
moved out from under a key where schema validation stripped it, to the namespace root where
it reaches the wire. Extra-body guardrails: object only, ≤16 KiB, secret-like and
prototype-pollution keys rejected before persist; schemas that strip unknown keys return
them as dropped keys surfaced as a Settings warning — never a silent drop.

**Learnings.**

- Emit namespaced options under the key the consumer itself derives, verified against SDK
  sources — an asymmetrical key fails with no error anywhere.
- Fixing a transport bug can activate a payload bug hiding underneath it: remove both
  together or the fix becomes the regression.
- Omission is part of the wire contract: unset fields must be absent at every call site.
- Static transcribed tables carrying source-and-date provenance, plus a validated raw
  passthrough escape hatch, absorb provider drift without dynamic capability discovery.

Study controls were the last feature-boundary piece still decided unilaterally by the app;
opening them up safely meant working next to some of the most fragile geometry in the
codebase.

## 010 — Customizable expound instructions

> **Status:** standing

**Goal.** Make the option list offered during expound — highlighting a passage in a chat
and branching off a model elaboration — fully user-managed: add/edit/remove entries with
required unique names and optional descriptions in Settings, expand built-in defaults from
three to five, and provide a restore-defaults escape hatch behind confirmation.

**Why.** The list lived as hardcoded constants; users could not extend it, so every
personal instruction style had to squeeze into a free-text box each time instead of
persisting as selectable one-click options.

**Outcome & reversals.** Shipped the same week it was specced. The list lives as a JSON
value under one settings key in the generic key-value table — no schema migration — seeded
idempotently at boot so upgrades gain the new built-ins untouched and customizations
survive restarts. Selected instruction names serialize verbatim onto branch records;
legacy toggle keys are mapped at read time and unknown strings preserved verbatim, so
branches created before edits or removals keep rendering their recorded labels — no
backfill ever rewrites history. Names validate trimmed, case-insensitively unique, length-
capped. Two constraints shaped everything around it: this feature's labels are pure
prompt/display strings riding atop deliberately frozen geometry — expound selections still
resolve through raw-markdown offsets via the source map plus DOM alignment; selections
touching generated content disable the menu; stale rows self-heal in memory only. That
frozen geometry itself encodes an earlier reversal recorded here for completeness: an
approach embedding links by mutating original markdown source was rejected outright
(offset cascades, content mutation) — substring heuristics, surround-style selection, and
full-span fallbacks are permanently banned, and the plan explicitly left selection/offset/
overlap paths untouched.

**Learnings.**

- A generic settings key absorbs new preference lists with zero migration when the value
  is loaded whole and never queried by column.
- Recording display names at creation time keeps history stable under later renames and
  removals — cheaper than ids or backfills.
- Read-time legacy mapping beats one-time data rewrites for backward compatibility.
- Features adjacent to fragile machinery should be scoped to plumbing; keeping label logic
  out of offset/alignment code avoided regression risk entirely.

*Arc B in retrospect:* every entry traded ad-hoc branching for data, derivation, or
adoption — shapes over identities, catalogs over code, one resolver over scattered maps,
user-managed strings over constants. Notably, the arc shipped almost entirely additive to
Arc A's contracts, validating them as a stable foundation. The one deep rewrite —
request-settings resolution — earned its deletion by replacing code the dialect research
proved defective.

## Arc C — Platform & delivery polish

The closing arc widened who can install Mayon and made the product legible at a glance —
and both features carry decision reversals handled the way we now consider standard:
built, evidenced, reviewed, and calmly revised.

## 011 — Podman compatibility

> **Status:** standing (one scope reversal inside the feature, same session)

**Goal.** Let self-hosters install and lifecycle-manage Mayon with Podman — containers
running rootless, without root privileges — while Docker remains the primary engine
everywhere: detection default, dev default, CI, release packaging. One installer and one
engine-neutral compose file serve both engines; no forked variants.

**Why.** The owner's own workstation is Podman-only; shell aliases help interactive
typing but are useless for non-interactive contexts — piped installs and npm scripts never
load them — so real binary-level engine resolution was required, not convenience.

**Outcome & reversals.** Shipped and merged. The installer resolves the engine in a fixed
order — explicit override → recorded preference file → auto-detection preferring Docker —
falling back if the preferred engine lacks working compose support. Every lifecycle
subcommand binds to the recorded engine thereafter: a missing engine dies with a clear
message naming the preference key rather than silently switching. The cross-engine hazard
— named volumes are engine-scoped and invisible to the other engine — is detected before
deploy, with interactive confirm defaulting to abort and a hard abort under non-interactive
stdin, so an empty fresh database can never masquerade as the user's data. Rootless
low-port attempts get engine-specific remediation guidance. The dev workflow gained the
same policy through one shared dispatcher script used structurally by all dev commands —
with the important nuance that this *secondary* dev support was itself a same-session
scope reversal: the clarification originally excluded dev entirely, and CI/release
packaging remain Docker-only permanently. Runtime code and app behavior were untouched.

**Learnings.**

- Engine-scoped storage turns "which engine created this volume" into the central
  correctness hazard, bigger than CLI compatibility.
- Persist the engine decision at creation time; it prevents silent divergence later.
- Non-interactive invocations invalidate interactive conveniences; selection logic must
  inspect real binaries.

## 012 — UI visual articulation pass

> **Status:** standing — three mid-flight owner reversals, all landed before merge

**Goal.** A restyling-and-affordance pass over every screen: exactly one warm accent hue
reserved for actionable emphasis (buttons, links, active nav, focus rings, focused
composer); a three-step surface hierarchy — canvas, panel, raised card; the composer as a
centered rounded card whose launchers immediately create persistent artifacts anchored to
the conversation; a home page with resume affordances; hover-revealed row actions;
connector-line tree carets; one shared row-card grammar for chat/quiz/lab lists;
stagger-fade motion honoring reduced-motion preferences; skeletons only past ~300 ms.

**Why.** Nothing looked clickable without trial and error; hierarchy was encoded nowhere
perceivable; powerful features (branching, quizzes, labs) were tribal knowledge. Hard
governing principles bounded the how: articulation comes from hairline borders and subtle
shadows — edges, not brightness — because the low text contrast is intentional eye
comfort, so flatness must never be fixed by raising text contrast; exactly one sans-serif
type family; everything persists, reinforcing the standing rule that interactions become
artifacts on the main screen rather than ephemeral modals; compress chrome without
amputating facts; one accent system-wide, status colors stay status-only.

**Outcome & reversals.** Landed through the feature branch and merged with all ten success
criteria verdicts PASS and test gates green. Three reversals were caught by the pass's own
evidence discipline and landed before merge: (1) the proposed warm-charcoal night theme —
fully built as a token-level hue shift at constant lightness — was ruled down to achromatic
grays ("stick to the gray palette, keeping the accent"), reverting neutrals at digit-
identical lightness with the accent trio surviving as the sole saturated family — proving
hairline-edge articulation carries hierarchy without warmth; (2) the serif typography
experiment was introduced and cut within the same effort, confirming the sans-serif ruling;
(3) the five-seed home starter chip set was reduced to a single explore-new-topic chip,
the removed seeds duplicating what composer launchers and the resume card already cover.
Launcher persistence was demonstrated as real database rows, honoring the artifacts-not-
modals principle. A pre-existing cold-load bootstrap race was reproduced during testing,
pinned as predating the feature, and flagged for follow-up.

**Learnings.**

- Depth reads through edges and shadow, never brightened text; preserving exact lightness
  made the achromatic revert risk-free.
- Tokenize experiments so an owner veto is a cheap revert, not a redesign.
- A hard persistence principle keeps shiny new affordances from minting ephemeral state.
- Per-story evidence captured before sign-off meant reversals cost almost nothing and left
  an auditable trail.

*Arc C in retrospect:* neither feature moved a schema; both changed how much of the system
users can see and steer. The repeated pattern — build the strong form, capture evidence,
let an explicit ruling trim it — is the project's decisive-method matured: reversals
stopped being failures once they stopped being expensive.

## Where the story stands

Twelve features in ten days of calendar time, with one recurring shape: invent narrowly,
prove broadly, revise without ceremony. The durable mechanics — typed entries, derived
states, written contracts, catalog-driven extensibility, offset-sanctified selection,
evidenced styling rulings — now function as the platform every future feature inherits.
The know-how distilled above is deliberately opinionated; when a future change contradicts
an entry here, update that entry in the same change — this document is a living decision
record, not a museum.
